chunks: From him, from Al-Haytham ibn Abi Mas'ruq, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to a man who came to him: 'Shall I guide you to a matter by which Allah will admit you to Paradise?' He said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Give from what Allah has given you.' He said: 'But what if I am more in need than the one to whom I give?' He said: 'Then help the oppressed.' He said: 'And what if I am weaker than the one I help?' He said: 'Then deal with the silly one (al-akhrak), meaning, indicate upon him (his affairs).' He said: 'What if I am sillier than the one I do this for?' He said: 'Then silence your tongue except from goodness.' Would it not please you that there should be a characteristic from these characteristics in you, pulling you to Paradise?

key_terms.أَشِرْ عَلَيْهِ: Indicate upon him / point out to him
key_terms.أَنِلْ: Give from what is given to you (charity/giving)
key_terms.الْأَخْرَقِ: The silly/foolish one (a specific term used in this context)

ai.seo_question: What is the hierarchy of good deeds from giving wealth to controlling the tongue according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi outlines a descending hierarchy of spiritual effort, culminating in 'silence of the tongue' (samt al-lisan) as the most accessible and foundational virtue for all believers, regardless of their capacity for wealth or strength. Shia scholars emphasize this progression as a practical guide for self-purification (tazkiyah), where guarding one's speech is the prerequisite for higher acts of justice and charity. The narration underscores that even the simplest act of speaking only good serves as a direct conduit to Paradise, highlighting the centrality of verbal discipline in Shia ethical teachings.
